title: Polymorphism
intro: Polymorphism lets one superclass reference call the right subclass method at run time (dynamic binding). It is what makes `Shape s = new Circle(); s.area();` work. It also explains why some things (fields, static, private and overloaded methods) are decided at compile time, and how casts can fail.

cards.title: Polymorphism = "many forms"
cards.body:
In OOP, polymorphism is the ability of **one object reference to refer to objects of different types**, with the **correct method chosen** according to where the object sits in the inheritance hierarchy.
**Overriding** is the tool that makes it possible: each subclass redefines `move()`, and the same call `animal.move()` gives different behaviour.

cards.title: Reference type vs object type: the remote and the TV
cards.body:
`<reference type> name = new <object type>();`
The **reference** (left side) is like a **remote control**: its buttons are only the methods the **reference type declares**. The **object** (right side) is the **TV**: it decides what actually happens when a button is pressed.

cards.title: Upcasting (always safe)
cards.body:
**Upcasting** is assigning a subclass object to a superclass (or any ancestor) variable. It is **implicit**: no cast is needed. It is always safe because of is-a: a Rectangle **is a** Shape.
The slides' rule: assigning a subclass reference to a superclass variable is safe, but referring to **subclass-only members** through it is a **compile error**.

cards.title: Dynamic binding (late binding)
cards.body:
**Binding** connects a method call to a method body. With **dynamic binding**, the choice is **delayed until run time** and based on the **actual object**, not the declared type. Java uses dynamic binding by default for instance methods.
It happens in two steps: the compiler checks that the method exists in the reference type, then the JVM picks the object's version.

cards.title: Static binding (early binding): decided at compile time
cards.body: **Static binding** fixes the method at **compile time**. In Java it applies to **private, final and static methods**, to the choice between **overloaded** methods, and to **fields** (data is never overridden; a subclass field with the same name just **hides** the parent's).

cards.title: Overloading is resolved statically
cards.body:
In the slides' StaticBindingTest, there are two overloaded `sort` methods: `sort(Collection)` and `sort(HashSet)`. A variable declared as `Collection c = new HashSet();` is passed in.
The compiler chooses the overload using the **declared type** (Collection), so the output is "Inside Collection sort method", even though the object is a HashSet.
keypoints: Overloading: compile time, uses declared types
Overriding: run time, uses the object type
Slides: takeAWalk(Cat) / takeAWalk(Lion) = overloading = static binding

cards.title: Downcasting and instanceof
cards.body:
**Downcasting** casts from a superclass to a subclass. It needs an **explicit cast**, and it only works if the object really **is** that subclass (or one of its descendants). Otherwise it throws a **ClassCastException** at run time.
`obj instanceof ClassName` returns true if obj is an instance of ClassName **or any of its descendant classes**. Use it to check before you cast.

cards.title: Compile error or ClassCastException?
cards.body:
Ask two questions:
1. **Compile time** (reference types only): Is the assignment upward? Then it's OK. Is it downward **without** a cast? That's a compile error. Are the types **unrelated** classes, like `(String) shape`? Compile error.
2. **Run time** (actual object): With a cast present, is the object really the target type? If not: **ClassCastException**.
cards.after: The slides' example: `Figure fig = new Figure(); Cylinder cy = fig;` is a **compile error** (needs a cast). `Cylinder cy = (Cylinder) fig;` compiles, but fails at run time. (The slides say the compiler never checks casts. In real Java it does reject casts between unrelated classes.)
keypoints: Missing cast on a downcast: compile error
Cast present, wrong object: ClassCastException
Unrelated class types: compile error

cards.title: Allowed assignments (slide summary)
cards.body: Here are the slides' four assignment rules, written as code:
cards.code:
Object ob = new Object();            // super to super: OK
String st = new String("x");         // sub to sub: OK
Object o2 = new String("x");         // sub to super: OK (upcast)
// o2.charAt(0);                     // compile error: Object has no charAt
// String s2 = new Object();         // super to sub: compile error
String s3 = (String) o2;             // explicit downcast: OK here
String s4 = (String) new Object();   // compiles, ClassCastException at run time
keypoints: Superclass variable can hold a subclass object
Subclass variable needs a cast (and the right object)

cards.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
cards.body:
Barbara Liskov (1988): **subtypes must be substitutable for their base types**. Any code written for a `Shape` must still behave correctly when it is given a Circle or a Rectangle.
This is the rule that makes polymorphism safe: a method like `void call(Animal animal) { animal.move(); }` works for every present and future subclass of Animal.
keypoints: If S is a subtype of T, an S can be used wherever a T is expected
Subclasses should not break what the superclass promises

cards.title: Three ways of method overriding (slides)
cards.body:
1. **Overriding a superclass method**: a subclass redefines a concrete method.
2. **Implementing an abstract method**: a subclass gives a body to an abstract method of an abstract class.
3. **Implementing an interface method**: a concrete class implements the methods of a Java interface.
All three can be called through a superclass or interface reference, with dynamic binding.
keypoints: Superclass method, abstract method, interface method
All three are resolved by dynamic binding

cards.title: Abstract methods in a hierarchy
cards.body: An abstract method has **no body**, and every concrete subclass must implement it. In the slides' example, Mammal doesn't implement `speak()`, so Mammal **must be abstract** too. Dog is concrete: it implements speak(), overrides move() and grow(), and inherits eat().
cards.code:
Mammal m = new Dog();
m.speak();   // Woof!
m.move();    // Dog move!
m.eat();     // Mammal eat!   (inherited)
m.grow();    // Dog grow!
cards.after: The output is the same through `Dog mDog` and through `Mammal m`, because the object is a Dog either way. (The slides' printed output says "Dog moves!" and so on, but the code prints "Dog move!".)
keypoints: Not implementing an inherited abstract method means the class must be abstract
`new Mammal()` is illegal; `Mammal m = new Dog()` is fine

cards.title: Benefits: simplicity and extensibility
cards.body:
**Simplicity**: code that works with a family of types talks only to the **base type**, and ignores type-specific details.
**Extensibility**: add a **new subclass** (Triangle) and the existing code that loops over `Shape` references works **without modification**.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body:
1. Thinking `a.subOnlyMethod()` works because the object has it. The compiler checks the **reference type**.
2. Expecting fields to be polymorphic. `a.name` uses the **reference type**.
3. Expecting static methods to be polymorphic. They are bound to the reference type.
4. Thinking a private parent method can be overridden. The child's method with the same name is a separate method.
5. Mixing up the compile error (missing cast or unrelated types) with the **run-time** ClassCastException.
6. Thinking overloading is dynamic. Overloads are chosen at **compile time** from the declared types.
keypoints: Compile time: reference type. Run time: object type (overridden methods only)
